stem: If \(A = \{x / x \in \mathrm{N},\ x \text{ is a factor of } 6\}\), \(B = \{x / x \in \mathrm{N},\ x \text{ is a factor of } 8\}\), find the \(A - B\) and \(B - A\).
\(A = \left\{\dfrac{1}{x} / x \in \mathrm{N},\ x < 8\right\}\), \(B = \left\{\dfrac{1}{2x} / x \in \mathrm{N},\ x \le 8\right\}\). Find \(A - B\) and \(B - A\).

If \(A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\), \(B = \{3, 4, 5, 6\}\), \(C = \{5, 6, 7, 8\}\), \(D = \{7, 8, 9, 10\}\) find i) \(A \cup B\) ii) \(A \cup B \cup C\) iii) \(B \cup C \cup D\). Are the sets A, B, C, D equivalent?
solution:
We have
i) \(A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\)
ii) \(A \cup B \cup C = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}\)
iii) \(B \cup C \cup D = \{3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10\}\)
As \(n(A) = n(B) = n(C) = n(D) = 4\), the sets A, B, C, D are equivalent.

stem: In a board examination, 40 students failed in Physics, 40 in Chemistry and 35. In Maths, 20 failed in Maths and Physics, 17 in Physics and Chemistry, 15 in Maths and Chemistry and 5 in all the three subjects. If 350 students appeared in the examination, how many of them did not fail in any subject?
solution:
Let P = set of students failed in Physics, C = set of students failed in Chemistry, M = set of students failed in Maths.
From figure 5.17, we have
\(n(X) = 350\), \(n(P) = 40\), \(n(C) = 40\), \(n(M) = 35\)
\(n(M \cap P) = 20\), \(n(P \cap C) = 17\), \(n(M \cap C) = 15\)
and \(n(M \cap P \cap C) = 5\)
The number of students who failed in at least one subject \(= n(M \cup P \cup C)\)
we have,
\(n(M \cup P \cup C) = n(M) + n(P) + n(C) - n(M \cap P) - n(P \cap C) - n(M \cap C) + n(M \cap P \cap C)\)
\(= 35 + 40 + 40 - 20 - 17 - 15 + 5 = 68\)
The number of students who did not fail in any subject \(= n(X) - n(M \cup P \cup C) = 350 - 68 = 282\)
_note: Printed punctuation defect in the stem: the book prints '40 students failed in Physics, 40 in Chemistry and 35. In Maths, 20 failed in Maths and Physics'. The intended reading is '...40 in Chemistry and 35 in Maths. 20 failed in Maths and Physics...', which is what the solution uses (n(M) = 35). Transcribed as printed. The printed solution also carries a Venn diagram (Fig. 5.17) whose regions read 8 (Physics only), 15 (Physics and Maths only), 5 (Maths only), 5 (all three), 10 (Maths and Chemistry only), 12 (Physics and Chemistry only), 13 (Chemistry only); the stem is answerable from its own numbers without the figure.

stem: A company produces three kinds of products A, B and C. The company studied the perference of 1600 consumers for these 3 products. It was found that the product A was liked by 1250, the product B was liked by 930 and product C was liked by 1000. The proudcts A and B were liked by 650, the products B and C were liked by 610 and the products C and A were liked by 700 consumers. None of the products were liked by 30 consumers. Find number of consumers who liked. i) All the three products ii) Only two of these products.
solution:
Given that totally 1600 consumers were studied. \(\therefore n(X) = 1600\), Let A be the set of all consumers who liked product A. Let B the set of all consumers who liked product B and C be the set of all consumers who liked product C.
\(n(A) = 1250\), \(n(B) = 930\), \(n(C) = 1000\).
\(n(A \cap B) = 650\), \(n(B \cap C) = 610\)
\(n(A \cap C) = 700\), \(n(A' \cap B' \cap C') = 30\)
i) \(n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(X) - n[(A \cup B \cup C)']\)
\(= n(X) - n(A' \cap B' \cap C') = 1600 - 30 = 1570\)
Since, \(n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A \cap B) - n(B \cap C) - n(C \cap A) + n(A \cap B \cap C)\)
\(\therefore 1570 = 1250 + 930 + 1000 - 650 - 610 - 700 + n(A \cap B \cap C)\)
\(\therefore n(A \cap B \cap C) = 1570 + 1960 - 3180\)
\(= 350\)
\(\therefore\) The number of consumers who liked all the three products is 350.
ii) \(n[(A \cap B) \cap C'] = n(A \cap B) - n[(A \cap B) \cap C]\)
\(\because n(P \cap Q') = n(P) - n[P \cap Q]\)
\(= 650 - 350 = 300\)
Similarly \(n(A' \cap B \cap C) = 610 - 350 = 260\)
and \(n(A \cap B' \cap C) = 700 - 350 = 350\)
\(\therefore\) The number of consumers who liked only two of the three products is
\(= n(A \cap B \cap C') + n(A \cap B' \cap C) + n(A' \cap B \cap C)\)
\(= 300 + 350 + 260 = 910\)
_note: Two spelling typos preserved as printed in the stem: 'perference' (preference) and 'proudcts' (products). In the printed solution the book also sets the prime outside the bracket in step i) as n[(A\cup B\cup C)]' and drops the leading n in 'Since, (A\cup B\cup C) = n(A) + ...'; both are typesetting slips and the solution here is transcribed with them corrected to the internally consistent form. The printed solution carries a Venn diagram (Fig. 5.18) labelling the regions A\cap B'\cap C', A'\cap B\cap C', A'\cap B'\cap C and A\cap B'\cap C'; the stem is answerable without it.

subtopic: Types of Sets and Number of Elements
stem: In a survey of 100 consumers 72 like product A and 45 like product B. Find the least and the most number that must have liked both products A and B.
solution:
Let \(n(A)\) and \(n(B)\) be number of consumers who like product A and B respectively, i.e. \(n(A) = 72\), \(n(B) = 45\).
Since
\(n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B) = 72 + 45 - n(A \cap B) = 117 - n(A \cap B)\).
But as only 100 consumers are surveyed. Therefore \(n(A \cup B) \le 100\) i.e. \(117 - n(A \cap B) \le 100\).
\(\therefore 117 - 100 \le n(A \cap B)\), \(17 \le n(A \cap B)\).
So the least number of consumers who like both the products is 17.
Since \(n(A \cap B) \le n(A)\), \(n(A \cap B) \le n(B)\), then
\(n(A \cap B) \le \min\{n(A), n(B)\} = \min\{72, 45\} = 45\). So the most number of consumers who like both products is 45.
_note: The printed solution spells 'proudct' for 'product'; written correctly here as it is prose in the solution, not the question.

stem: If \((x+1, y-2) = (3, 1)\) find the value of \(x\) and \(y\).
solution:
Since the order pairs are equal, the coresponding elements are equal.
\(\therefore x + 1 = 3\) and \(y - 2 = 1\)
\(\therefore x = 2\) and \(y = 3\)

We have \(A \times B = \{(1, 2), (1, 3), (3, 2), (3, 3), (5, 2), (5, 3)\}\) and \(B \times A = \{(2, 1), (2, 3), (2, 5), (3, 1), (3, 3), (3, 5)\}\)

stem: A and B are two sets given in such a way that \(A \times B\) contains 6 elements. If three elements of \(A \times B\) are \((1, 3)\), \((2, 5)\) and \((3, 3)\), find its remaining elements.
solution:
Since \((1, 3)\), \((2, 5)\) and \((3, 3)\) are in \(A \times B\) it follows that 1, 2, 3 are elements of A and 3, 5 are elements of B. As \(A \times B\) contains 6 elements and if we let
\(A = \{1, 2, 3\}\) and \(B = \{3, 5\}\), then
\(A \times B = \{(1, 3), (1, 5), (2, 3), (2, 5), (3, 3), (3, 5)\}\) giving \(n(A \times B) = 6\).
Hence, the remaining elements of \(A \times B\) are \((1, 5)\), \((2, 3)\) and \((3, 5)\).

stem: Let \(R\) be a relation on \(Q\), defined by \(R = \{(a, b) / a, b \in Q \text{ and } a - b \in Z\}\). Show that \(R\) is an equivalence relation.
solution:
Given \(R = \{(a, b) / a, b \in Q \text{ and } a - b \in Z\}\)

i) Let \(a \in Q\) then \(a - a = 0 \in Z\)

\(\therefore (a, a) \in R\)

So, \(R\) is reflexive.

ii) \((a, b) \in R \Rightarrow (a - b) \in Z\)

i.e. \((a - b)\) is an integer

\(\Rightarrow -(a - b)\) is an integer

\(\Rightarrow (b - a)\) is an integer

\(\Rightarrow (b, a) \in R\)

Thus \((a, b) \in R \Rightarrow (b, a) \in R\)

\(\therefore R\) is symmetric.

iii) \((a, b) \in R\) and \((b, c) \in R\)

\(\Rightarrow (a - b)\) is an integer and \((b - c)\) is an integer

\(\Rightarrow \{(a - b) + (b - c)\}\) is an integer

\(\Rightarrow (a - c)\) is an integer

\(\Rightarrow (a, c) \in R\)

Thus \((a, b) \in R\) and \((b, c) \in R \Rightarrow (a, c) \in R\)

\(\therefore R\) is transitive.

Thus, \(R\) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

\(\therefore R\) is an equivalence relation.
_note: Printed on p-14 (book p.101), left column, 'Ex. 1:' of the 'Illustrative examples' under the unnumbered sub-heading 'Equivalence relation:', which sits inside section 5.2.7 Types of relations (begun on p-13, right column).

stem: Show that the relation "is congruent to" on the set of all triangles in a plane is an equivalence relation.
solution:
Let \(S\) be the set of all triangles in a plane. Then, the congruence relation on \(S\) is

i) Reflexive, since \(\Delta \cong \Delta\) for every \(\Delta \in S\)

ii) Symmetric, since \(\Delta_1 \cong \Delta_2 \Rightarrow \Delta_2 \cong \Delta_1\) for all \(\Delta_1, \Delta_2 \in S\).

iii) Transitive, since \(\Delta_1 \cong \Delta_2\) and \(\Delta_2 \cong \Delta_3\), then \(\Delta_1 \cong \Delta_3\) for all \(\Delta_1, \Delta_2, \Delta_3 \in S\). Hence, the given relation is an equivalence relation.
_note: Printed on p-14 (book p.101), 'Ex. 2 :' under the 'Equivalence relation:' sub-heading of section 5.2.7. The stem and parts i)-ii) are at the foot of the left column; part iii) continues at the top of the right column.

stem: Show that \(R = \{(a, b) : a, b \in Z,\ a \equiv b \ (\mathrm{mod}\ m)\}\) is an equivalence relation.
solution:
Since \(a - a = 0\) is divisible by \(m\)

\(\therefore a \equiv a \ (\mathrm{mod}\ m)\) \(\therefore R\) is reflexive.

If \(a \equiv b \ (\mathrm{mod}\ m)\) i.e. \(a - b\) is divisible by \(m\) then \(b - a\) is also divisible by \(m\)

i.e. \(b \equiv a \ (\mathrm{mod}\ m)\). \(\therefore R\) is symmetric.

If \(a \equiv b \ (\mathrm{mod}\ m)\) and \(b \equiv c \ (\mathrm{mod}\ m)\)

i.e. \(a - b\) is divisible by \(m\) and \(b - c\) is divisible by \(m\).

Then \(a - c = a - b + b - c = (a - b) + (b - c)\) is also divisible by \(m\). i.e. \(a \equiv c \ (\mathrm{mod}\ m)\).

\(\therefore R\) is transitive.

So, \(R\) is an equivalence relation.
_note: Printed on p-14 (book p.101), right column, labelled simply 'Ex.' under the unnumbered sub-heading 'Congruence Modulo:', which sits inside section 5.2.7 Types of relations. The book prints 'transitivie' for 'transitive' (spelling slip only).

context: Solve the following inequalities and write the solution set using interval notation.
solution:
subtracting, 4, we get

[Note that, as we do not know value of \(x\), we do not multiply by \((x - 3)\)]

\(\frac{x}{x-3} - 4 \ge 0\)

\(\frac{x - 4(x-3)}{x-3} \ge 0\)

\(\frac{x - 4x + 12}{x-3} \ge 0\)

\(\frac{-3x + 12}{x-3} \ge 0\)

\(\frac{-3(x-4)}{x-3} \ge 0\)

Dividing by \(-3\), we get

Say \(p(x) = \frac{x-4}{x-3} \le 0\)

Take \(x = 3, 4\) as critical points. It divides number line into 3 regions as follows.

| Regions | \((x \le 3)\) | \((3 \le x \le 4)\) | \((x \ge 4)\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Test Points | \(2\) | \(3.5\) | \(5\) |
| Sign of \(x - 4\) | \(-\)ve | \(-\)ve | \(+\)ve |
| Sign of \(x - 3\) | \(-\)ve | \(+\)ve | \(+\)ve |
| Sign of \(p(x)\) | \(p(x) > 0\) Except at \(x = 3\) | \(p(x) < 0\) | \(p(x) > 0\) |

The solution set is \((x < 3)\) and \((x \ge 4)\). So \(x \in (-\infty, 3) \cup [4, \infty)\).

Here \(x = 3\) is not in the solution set, as it makes denominator 0.
_note: Printed defect, transcribed as printed (NOT repaired). The book's own derivation ends at p(x) = (x-4)/(x-3) <= 0 and its own sign table marks p(x) < 0 only in the middle region, so the solution set should be (3, 4]; the printed conclusion (-inf, 3) U [4, inf) is the region where p(x) >= 0, i.e. the opposite. Numerical check on the ORIGINAL inequality x/(x-3) >= 4: x = 3.5 gives 7 (satisfies, but is excluded by the printed answer) and x = 5 gives 2.5 (fails, but is included by the printed answer). Secondary defect: the printed region headers use <= / >= so the three regions overlap at the critical points x = 3 and x = 4, and x = 3 is not admissible at all.
